newsitem.title: GREECE: GREECE RISKS SEA OF LAW SUITS IF FRN TAX ADOPTED.
newsitem.headline: GREECE RISKS SEA OF LAW SUITS IF FRN TAX ADOPTED.

text.p: Greece will be hit with a sea of lawsuits if the government adopts a controversial withholding tax on outstanding coupons of FRNs, local and foreign bankers told Reuters.
The issue is whether the government would use the gross 12-month T-bill rate or the lower after-tax rate in fixing coupons of outstanding three-, six- and seven-year FRNs.
A witholding tax on T-bills is expected to be adopted as a means to enhance tax revenues in the 1997 budget.

"All our foreign investor clients are determined to protect their interests, if necessary in court, because they are convinced that a different interpretation of the interest rate of the benchmark 12-month T-bill used for FRN repricing cannot stand in a court of law," said Harris Makkas, deputy general manager and country treasurer at the Bank of America in Athens.
There are 10 general terms stated in the back of Greek FRNs. The eigth term states that interest payments on the paper are not subject to any tax whatsoever.
The second term states that the interest rate of the annual T-bill is the base rate used along with a spread to set FRN coupons, making no mention of the T-bill yield.
"Do you think we are going to sit idle if Greek officials decide not to play by the rules?" asked a London-based investor. "Of course we will take them to court."
A number of local and foreign dealers reported similar action by investors in several EU countries.
"Does anybody down there care about credibility?" asked another dealer based abroad.

Prime minister Costas Simitis, National Economy and Finance Minister Yannos Papandoniou, Deputy Finance Ministers Nick Chrystodoulakis and George Drys and Deputy National Economy Minister Christos Pachtas are meeting today to put the final touches on the 1997 budget and take up the tax issues on treasuries and derivatives. --Dimitris Kontogiannis, Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
